en: Joy, beautiful spark of the gods,
daughter from Elysium,
we enter, drunk with fire,
heavenly one, your sanctuary.
Your magic binds again
what the sword of fashion divided;
beggars become brothers of princes
where your gentle wing lingers.
Be embraced, millions!
This kiss to the whole world!
Brothers – above the tent of stars
a loving father must dwell.
Whoever has succeeded in the great throw
of being a friend's friend;
whoever has won a lovely wife,
let him mix in his rejoicing!
Yes – whoever calls even one soul
his own on the round of the earth!
And whoever never could, let him steal
away weeping from this league!
Whatever dwells in the great ring,
let it pay homage to sympathy!
To the stars she leads,
where the Unknown One is enthroned.
All beings drink joy
at the breasts of nature;
all the good, all the wicked
follow her trail of roses.
Kisses she gave us, and vines,
a friend, proven in death.
Sensual pleasure was given to the worm,
and the cherub stands before God.
You fall down, millions?
Do you sense the Creator, world?
Seek him above the tent of stars;
above the stars he must dwell.
Joy is the name of the strong spring
in eternal nature.
Joy, joy drives the wheels
in the great clock of the worlds.
She lures flowers out of the seeds,
suns out of the firmament,
she rolls spheres in the spaces
that the seer's tube does not know!
Glad, as his suns fly
through the splendid plain of heaven,
run your course, brothers,
joyful as a hero to victory.
From the fiery mirror of truth
she smiles at the seeker.
To the steep hill of virtue
she guides the sufferer's path.
On the sunlit mountain of faith
one sees her banners wave;
through the crack of burst coffins
one sees her stand in the choir of angels.
Endure bravely, millions!
Endure for the better world!
Up there above the tent of stars
a great God will reward.
Gods cannot be repaid;
it is beautiful to be like them.
Grief and poverty, let them come forward
to rejoice with the joyful.
Let grudge and revenge be forgotten,
our mortal enemy be forgiven.
No tear shall press him,
no remorse gnaw at him.
Let our book of debts be destroyed!
the whole world reconciled!
Brothers – above the tent of stars
God judges as we have judged.
Joy bubbles in goblets;
in the golden blood of the grape
cannibals drink gentleness,
despair drinks heroic courage – –
Brothers, fly from your seats
when the full wine-glass goes round;
let the foam spurt up to heaven:
this glass to the good spirit.
Him whom the whirl of the stars praises,
whom the seraph's hymn extols:
this glass to the good spirit
above the tent of stars up there!
Firm courage in heavy suffering,
help where innocence weeps,
eternity to oaths that are sworn,
truth towards friend and foe,
manly pride before the thrones of kings, –
brothers, even if it cost goods and blood –
to merit its crowns,
downfall to the brood of lies!
Close the holy circle tighter,
swear by this golden wine
to be true to the vow,
swear it by the judge of the stars!
Rescue from tyrants' chains,
magnanimity even to the villain,
hope on the deathbeds,
mercy on the scaffold!
The dead too shall live!
Brothers, drink and join in:
all sinners shall be forgiven,
and hell shall be no more.
A cheerful hour of parting!
sweet sleep in the shroud!
Brothers – a gentle sentence
from the mouth of the judge of the dead!
notes: This is the 1786 text (Thalia), not the 1803 revision Beethoven set in 1824: lines 1.6-1.7 here read 'what the sword of fashion divided; beggars become brothers of princes', where 1803 has 'what fashion strictly divided; all men become brothers'. The 1803 text also drops the last stanza pair (17-18 here). Do not present this translation as the words of Beethoven's Ninth.
Spelling is the 1786 printing's (Elisium, Heiligthum, Schwerd, seyn, Simpathie, tronet, kraißt, Todten); translated as the modern words.
Stanzas alternate solo and chorus: the even-numbered four-line stanzas are the chorus ('Chor') of the original printing.
line 3.1: 'der große Wurf' is literally 'the great throw' (of dice), i.e. the great stroke of fortune; kept literal.
line 4.1: 'der große Ring' (the great ring) is the round world or the whole of creation.
line 4.2: 'Simpathie' in the 18th-century sense: the attraction or fellow-feeling that binds all beings, not pity.
line 5.7: 'Wollust' is sensual pleasure or delight (not only 'lust' in the modern sense).
line 7.5: 'Keimen' are seeds or germs; 'buds' is also possible.
line 7.8: 'des Sehers Rohr' is the seer's (astronomer's) tube, i.e. the telescope.
line 8.2: 'Plan' here is the old sense 'plain, level expanse', not 'design'; 'plan' is possible but less likely.
line 9.8: the verb 'sieht man' (one sees) carries over from line 9.6; supplied as 'one sees her stand'.
line 13.4: the verb 'trinken' (drink) carries over from line 13.3; supplied once.
line 13.6: 'der volle Römer' is a Römer, a large stemmed wine-glass (English 'rummer'); 'kraißt' = 'kreist', goes round.
line 15.6: 'gält' es Gut und Blut' = 'were it to cost property and life (blood)'.
line 15.7: 'Dem Verdienste seine Kronen' = to merit (desert) its crowns, i.e. let merit be crowned.
line 17.4: 'Hochgericht' is the place of execution, the gallows or scaffold.
line 16.4: 'Sternenrichter' is literally 'star-judge', the judge above (or of) the stars.
